Battery arguments I think that the battery of iPhones is generally very good, and it’s not just about how many mAh the battery has. Samsung has larger batteries for many devices, for example, 5,000 mAh, but a larger battery capacity does not automatically mean that the phone will last longer. Apple is developing its own processor, iOS and energy management very closely together. As a result, the hardware and software are very well coordinated and the power consumption can be controlled efficiently. Especially the A-chips from Apple are very powerful and at the same time energy efficient, so that an iPhone can sometimes achieve a very good runtime with a smaller battery. In addition, iOS manages background processes and apps in a very controlled manner, which means that less energy can be lost in standby. Apple also has the advantage that the company can develop both the hardware and the operating system itself and thus optimise the entire system. Functions such as optimised charging also help to save the battery in the long term. Therefore, I would not simply say that an iPhone always has a longer battery life than a Samsung, but that Apple uses the existing battery very efficiently. In the end, it depends not only on the size of the battery, but on the interplay of battery, processor, display, mobile modem and software. It is precisely with this combination that I see one of the great strengths of the iPhone. Strong arguments for Apple Maps 1. Data protection is serious: Apple does not build a motion profile for advertising. Your routes, searches and places are not tracked in a personalised way. For many, this is a huge plus. 2. Perfect integration with the iPhone: Everything runs seamlessly on iOS Siri, Lock Screen Navigation, Apple Watch vibrations for turn-by-turn directions, CarPlay — it all feels like one piece. 3. Clear, calm navigation: Apple Maps is deliberately minimalistic. Less overloaded information, better readability while driving. Many find that more relaxed and safer. 4. Realistic 3D views & “Look Around”: In supported cities, the 3D models are extremely detailed. “Look Around” is Apple’s version of Street View - often more fluid and with better image quality. 5. Better Lane Guidance & Traffic Lights: In many regions, Apple Maps shows accurate lanes, zebra crossings, and traffic lights. Especially in complex intersections, this is worth gold. 6. Offline maps (since iOS 17+): You can download entire regions and navigate without the Internet — conveniently abroad or with poor reception. 7. Less battery consumption: Due to the close system integration, the energy consumption is often lower than with Google Maps. 5000 mAh ≠ Battery life – Apple shows Samsung how to do it! I mean that even the iPhone 16 Pro Max with under 5000 mAh the latest S26 Ultra with 5000 mAh defeated. text_raw: Having read some comments posted here and there, it's becoming increasingly clear to me that some people either didn't have use for or maybe never even perceived the full range of uses for the Bluetooth s-pen. So here's some explanation from a bluetooth s-pen devotee. Some have told us to just use our fingers for navigation, but if that was the only way we liked to navigate we wouldn't be complaining about being limited to it. We PREFER using the s-pen for some things. For example, the s-pen can make it way easier to be precise when selecting text, or to drag and drop, or to create handwriting or visual art. Voice commands to take photos make NOISE, and sometimes we don't want to disturb the people or wildlife around us with noise when we're trying to take a picture. Palm detection isn't always viable or convenient - for example, I've used Bluetooth s-pens to photograph the undercarriages of cars and the back sides of and spaces behind and inside of major appliances for informational purposes where even if I could stick my palm in the space it would be too close for the phone to perceive it. I've used it to photograph my cats and dogs and even camera shy friends and family (who would likely have changed position if I had moved to use a palm gesture or made noise to issue a voice command). I've photographed the tops of things that I can't come close to seeing when I'm standing on the floor but can juuust barely hold my phone high enough to aim the camera at, and while I may not be able to see the shutter button on the phone in those situations, I can hold the s-pen in my other hand and use it to trigger the shutter. Also, using the palm only works with the selfie camera, so if you want to use your main camera the palm is a no-go. Regarding SD cards - it can be much cheaper to buy a one terabyte SD card than it is to upgrade to one terabyte of storage on your phone, and even if your phone becomes irreparably damaged you might be able to rescue the card, and if you manage to fill one card up you can switch it out for another card instead of having to transfer the data from your phone to the cloud (which will be an additional cost) or your laptop or whatever and then delete it from your phone. Not my thing, but I can see how it could be useful to some people. Regarding using the USB port as a headphone jack...I got nothing. I find true wireless Bluetooth headsets much preferable to wired headsets, but maybe I've overlooked something on that issue.

Now, I expect, to some degree, that this will be addressed with the switch to TSMC from Samsung architecture. And with that, thermal issues impact battery health and longevity. Because, at least in the states, Samsung uses Qualcomm, not Exynos or other in-house fabrications. I actually like these phones. But you can’t ignore the realities. In closing - you have to remember that Apple has been integrating custom processors on their iPhones for years and have had their fair share of generation processors that were stove-top sizzlers. Same with Qualcomm and their Snapdragons. But both companies have continued to develop and refine those issues.
